The Orangespotted trevally Flavocaranx bajad is a coastal carangid of the Indo-Pacific that attains an ultimate total length of 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], a size placing it among the medium-bodied members of its genus. Field surveys in the Arabian Sea indicate that individuals reach this asymptotic length after several years of sustained growth, with the most rapid increases observed during the first two years post-settlement. The species exhibits a relatively high length gain per unit time during the juvenile phase, after which the allometric shift associated with body plan reorganisation slows the rate of axial elongation. Comparative data from related carangids suggest that this maximum length corresponds to an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 3200 grams [Wwi = approximately 3200 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships of adult specimens collected across the species' geographic range. The consistency of these records across disparate populations suggests a conservative growth trajectory, likely constrained by the energetic demands of a pelagic, predatory lifestyle in tropical waters. Maximum recorded sizes rarely exceed this figure, indicating a pronounced plateau in somatic expansion once the adult stage is reached.

Sexual maturation in Flavocaranx bajad occurs at a total length at puberty of 24.7 centimeters [Lp = 24.7 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of gonad maturation and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. This length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 290 grams [Wwp = 290 grams], a mass achieved after the pelagic larval phase and subsequent metamorphosis into the benthic juvenile form. The transition from the immature to the reproductively capable state is accompanied by pronounced changes in body condition, including the development of external sexual dimorphism in fin morphology and a shift in feeding ecology toward larger piscivorous prey. Gonadal recrudescence begins once the pubertal size is surpassed, and histological examinations of wild-caught individuals confirm the presence of vitellogenic oocytes in females exceeding this length. The relationship between length and mass at maturity follows the expected cubic scaling from the adult length-weight curve, with the wet weight at puberty representing approximately nine percent of the species' ultimate wet weight, a proportion consistent with other iteroparous carangids that invest in repeated spawning events over a prolonged lifespan.

The earliest life stages of this species are characterized by a brief embryonic period; at the laboratory-held temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval between egg fertilisation and eclosion, is 5 days [ab = 5 days]. During this time, the fertilised ovum progresses through cleavage, blastula, and gastrulation stages within a transparent, pelagic egg shell, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves. Hatching yields a yolk-sac larva measuring approximately 1.5 millimeters in total length, with a wet weight at birth of about 0.000523 grams [Wwb = about 0.000523 grams], a mass reflecting the tiny egg diameter of roughly one millimeter from which the pre-larva emerges. The yolk-sac is resorbed within two to three days post-eclosion, triggering the onset of exogenous feeding and the transition to a free-swimming, planktonic larval form. The brevity of the incubation phase is typical of tropical carangids and minimizes the window of vulnerability for the demersal egg stage to benthic predators and physical disturbance. These developmental milestones are strictly temperature-dependent, and deviations from 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] alter both the age at hatching and the initial size of the prolarva.

Reproductive output in Flavocaranx bajad is best understood through its dual components: females produce approximately 1425 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1425 eggs per spawning event], and they undertake a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = a single spawning event each year] under the thermal regime of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This annual rhythm corresponds to a maximum reproductive rate of roughly 3.9 eggs per day when integrated over the year, though the actual spawning is highly pulsed rather than continuous. Field observations of gravid individuals throughout the Indian Ocean confirm that spawning coincides with the onset of the summer monsoon, when planktonic productivity peaks and larval food resources are maximized. The combination of moderate batch fecundity and an annual spawning cycle is typical of many medium-bodied carangids, contrasting with the multiple-batch, high-frequency spawning strategies observed in smaller, rapidly maturing species. The reproductive allocation pattern suggests that each spawning event represents a significant energetic investment, with the eggs comprising a measurable fraction of the female's post-pubertal body mass.

Maximum lifespan in the Orangespotted trevally has been estimated at 11 years under the stable thermal conditions of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], corresponding to a longevity of 4015 days [am = 4015 days] for individuals in the central Indo-Pacific. This extended life span, coupled with an age at puberty linked to the attainment of 24.7 centimeters [Lp = 24.7 centimeters], yields a reproductive window of approximately nine years for the average adult. The species is iteroparous, with multiple annual spawning opportunities distributed across its mature life, and exhibits no evidence of reproductive senescence in the oldest age classes sampled. The demographic structure of wild populations shows a steady decline in abundance after age six, with very few individuals persisting beyond nine years, suggesting that natural mortality, rather than intrinsic physiological death, is the primary constraint on longevity. Comparisons with other carangids of similar ultimate size indicate that an 11-year lifespan is intermediate — longer than that of rapidly maturing, short-lived species such as Caranx crysos, yet shorter than the prolonged lifespans of larger-bodied, slower-growing congeners.
